GPU and ASIC power remain nearly equally important
Our bottom-up model is also built up for AMD and each major ASIC customer rather 
than applying NVIDIA economics across the industry. Chips per rack, system power, BBU/
CBU architecture, high-voltage topology, dedicated power-rack requirements and 
component content all vary by customer.  We estimate GPU systems from NVIDIA and 
AMD represent approximately 59% of AI power TAM in 2025, 58% in 2026 and 56% in 
2027, before falling to approximately 51% in 2028 and ending at 54% in 2030. ASIC 
systems therefore represent roughly 40–50% of industry power TAM throughout most 
of the forecast.
In dollar terms, GPU power TAM rises from US$3.9bn in 2025 to US$49.2bn in 2030, 
while ASIC power TAM increases from US$2.7bn to US$42.0bn. The architectures differ
—AWS, Google, Meta, Microsoft and OpenAI will not necessarily converge on NVIDIA’s 
exact rack implementation—but the fundamental power problem is common: more 
accelerator watts require greater conversion, protection, distribution, storage/
smoothing and downstream voltage conversion while the move up in rack compute 
density through more dies per package and more chips per rack is driving the 
OCP standards move toward power racks and native 800VDC architectures like NVIDIA.
This breadth is important for the investment case. The power TAM is ultimately tied to 
industry AI watts deployed, rather than requiring any single GPU vendor, ASIC program 
or rack standard to dominate the market. We would be explicit that the largest 
uncertainties are not all in the same direction. Accelerator shipment timing can move 
rack deployment between years; accelerators per rack can reduce rack counts even 
while increasing watts per rack; package and system TDP can move the GW 
denominator materially; and BBU/CBU attachment, power-rack sharing ratios, ±400V 
versus single-bus 800V topology and eventual SST penetration can all change content 
per watt.

The 169% and 115% growth rates we currently estimate for 2026 and 2027 could shift 
with product ramps without changing the central conclusion: the AI power market is 
moving from tens of kilowatts per rack toward hundreds of kilowatts and ultimately 
megawatt-class systems, while the architecture simultaneously adds new conversion, 
protection, storage and distribution content.
The critical point is that our US$91bn estimate is not predicated on extrapolating today’s 
rack BOM. It reflects a bottom-up view of how many accelerator systems are deployed, 
how much power those systems consume, where the power electronics sit and what 
hardware is required to deliver each IT watt through successive rack architectures.

AI Power TAM Sensitivities: IT GW is the primary TAM 
driver; architecture determines the upside around it
The two principal sensitivities to our AI Power TAM are annual IT capacity deployed and 
power-system content per supported IT watt. At a constant content per watt, a 10% 
change in our 104.5GW 2030 deployment assumption changes TAM by approximately 
US$9.1bn. Conversely, at our modelled 104.5GW of annual IT deployments, a US$0.05/
W change in blended power-system content changes 2030 TAM by approximately US
$5.2bn.
The sensitivities are not completely independent. Higher rack power can increase IT GW 
while simultaneously changing the required power architecture and therefore content 
per watt; conversely, slower deployment of high-density systems can reduce both the 
GW denominator and penetration of more content-rich power racks. We therefore view 
the sensitivity tables as illustrating the magnitude of individual drivers.
Near-term TAM is most sensitive to IT GW deployed
Our 2027 base case assumes 50.8GW of annual IT capacity and US$0.75 of power-
system content per IT watt, producing approximately US$38.2bn of TAM. Around this 
base case, each incremental 1GW of IT deployments adds roughly US$0.75bn of annual 
TAM, or approximately 2% of the TAM level. A US$0.01/W change in blended content 
adds approximately US$0.5bn, or around 1.3%.
The impact on the year-on-year growth rate is larger because the 2026 TAM base 
remains relatively small. An additional 1GW in 2027 adds approximately 4.2 percentage 
points to TAM growth, while an additional US$0.01/W of content adds approximately 
2.9 percentage points. This reinforces our view that the magnitude and timing of AI 
hardware deployments remain the most important variables for the 2026–27 inflection; 
widespread native 800V adoption is not required for a strong 2027 outcome.

Component price erosion is a risk, but rising system power and 
architectural upgrades mitigate the impact
Competitive pricing is another risk as conventional PSU volumes scale, more suppliers 
qualify and mature specifications such as Blackwell's mainstream 5.5kW PSUs become 
more standardized. However, our bottom-up BOM suggests that single-component 
price erosion has a more modest effect on total system content than changes in IT GW or 
architecture, because power content is increasingly distributed across conversion, 
storage, protection, distribution, controls and downstream DC/DC and also the PSUs are 
upgrading to higher complexity specs moving to 18.3kW and beyond.
Our VR200 integrated-power case contains approximately US$170k of rack power 
content using a PSU-module assumption of roughly US$0.13/W and BBU content of 
roughly US$0.20/W. Reducing PSU pricing by US$0.02/W lowers modelled rack power 
content by approximately 5%, while a US$0.05/W reduction in BBU pricing reduces 
total rack content by approximately 4%.
For the investment case, conventional PSU pricing on mature generations can face 
competitive pressure without invalidating the broader power TAM, particularly as 
additional content pools emerge in high-voltage distribution, protection, energy storage 
and near-silicon conversion. For individual suppliers unable to gain early qualification on 
newer generations of hardware, however, price erosion can still have a larger earnings 
impact depending on product mix and market share.

Storage attachment is a larger architectural swing factor than storage 
pricing alone
BBU and CBU content is less standardized than front-end conversion because 
attachment depends on the resilience architecture selected by the data-center operator. 
A deployment retaining centralized UPS infrastructure may need relatively little rack-
level battery capacity, while hyperscale systems requiring local ride-through or source-
transfer support may attach materially more storage.
For VR200, our base case assumes roughly 50% BBU attachment at US$0.20/W. At that 
assumption, attach-weighted BBU content is approximately US$25.6k per system, 
contributing materially to the roughly US$170k total power BOM. Holding BBU pricing 
constant, moving attachment from 50% to 30% lowers modeled rack content by 
approximately 6%, while increasing attachment to 70% raises content by a similar 
amount. Moving across the much wider 10–100% attachment range produces a 
materially larger swing.
We therefore view BBU penetration as an architectural assumption rather than simply 
another ASP assumption. Greater upstream pooling of storage represents downside to 
rack-level BBU attachment, while increasing requirements for local ride-through, fast 
source transfer and workload stability provide upside. Importantly, lower rack-level BBU 
content does not necessarily imply proportionately lower total data-center storage 
content if capacity is instead centralized into DC UPS or BESS.

SST adoption is the largest out-year architecture sensitivity
The largest architecture-specific swing in our 2030 NVIDIA model is SST penetration. 
Our base case assumes approximately 45% SST penetration, resulting in NVIDIA power 
TAM of approximately US$41.8bn in 2030. Holding the underlying hardware forecast 
constant, eliminating SST adoption reduces modelled NVIDIA TAM to approximately US
$37.2bn, while increasing penetration to 90% raises TAM to approximately US$46.4bn 
under our base SST-content assumption.  
The 45% SST assumption contributes roughly US$4.6bn of incremental NVIDIA power 
TAM versus a no-SST scenario. Each additional 15ppt of SST penetration around our 
base case moves annual TAM by roughly US$1.5bn, although the precise impact varies 
with the assumed power content of an SST-equipped architecture.

SST penetration also has a disproportionate effect on the out-year growth profile. At our 
base content assumption, 2030 NVIDIA TAM growth is approximately 24% with 45% 
SST penetration, versus roughly 10% without SST adoption and approximately 38% at 
90% penetration. 
This highlights why we treat SST separately from our nearer-term 800V thesis: 2026–27 
growth is driven primarily by rapidly rising IT GW and rack power, 2028-29 by power 
rack upgrades and the 2029–30 and beyond growth profile is increasingly sensitive to 
which architecture ultimately wins and how much upstream transformation content 
migrates into the power-electronics opportunity.
SST should also be viewed as a net-content rather than gross-content opportunity. As 
discussed earlier, some upstream SST value displaces conventional front-end rectification 
and transformation. The relevant investment question is therefore not only whether SST 
is adopted, but which suppliers capture the larger engineered system as value migrates 
upstream and which are more impacted by displaced power conversion content closer to 
the rack.

Near-term TAM is driven by GW; architecture matters increasingly in the 
out-years
The sensitivity work reinforces three conclusions: 
1. IT GW deployed remains the largest determinant of total TAM, particularly 
through the 2026–27 ramp.
2. A broader power BOM limits the impact of competitive price erosion in any 
individual component, particularly for vendors able to migrate toward newer, 
higher-content architectures. 
3. Architecture increasingly determines the out-years opportunity: storage 
attachment, external power-rack penetration and particularly SST can materially 
alter both content/watt and the distribution of value across suppliers.
Our US$91bn 2030 estimate does not require every platform to migrate to the most 
content-rich architecture. Rather, the sensitivity work suggests the AI power thesis is 
fundamentally a watts thesis first and an architecture thesis second: rising IT GW 
expands the addressable market, while external power racks, storage and ultimately SST 
determine how much incremental power-electronics content is captured around those 
watts and which suppliers capture it.
Competitive landscape: who captures the 
expanding AI power stack?
Convergence across the white-space and grey-space
The rapid increase in AI rack power is reshaping the competitive landscape across the 
data-center power ecosystem. Historically, white-space suppliers focused on server 
PSUs, rack-level power shelves and board-level conversion, while grey-space vendors 
supplied UPS, switchgear, transformers and facility-level distribution. Higher-voltage DC 
architectures increasingly blur this distinction. Bulk AC/DC conversion, energy storage, 
protection and distribution progressively migrate upstream from the IT rack into 
dedicated power racks, rows and ultimately facility-level systems, while high-ratio DC/

DC and point-of-load conversion move closer to the accelerator.
We therefore see competitive advantage shifting from leadership in an individual power 
component toward breadth across the power stack, qualification with the major AI 
platforms, system-level control capability and the ability to scale from rack-level products 
into multi-MW power systems. Importantly, the opportunity does not accrue uniformly. 
Some suppliers gain incremental content as new layers of power electronics are added, 
while others risk having mature low-voltage conversion content displaced as conversion 
becomes more centralized.

Historically the white-space and grey-space suppliers operated in relatively separate 
parts of the data-center electrical chain. We expect that separation to narrow as higher-
voltage DC architectures mature. Grey-space incumbents are increasingly extending into 
rack-adjacent HVDC systems, while leading white-space suppliers are moving upstream 
into power racks, power centers and potentially medium-voltage conversion.
The key distinction therefore becomes less about where a supplier historically operated 
and more about how many stages of the architecture transition it can monetize. Delta 
has perhaps the broadest position spanning rack PSUs, DC/DC, energy storage, HVDC 
power racks, thermal management and upstream power conversion. Vertiv, Schneider 
and Eaton approach the market from the opposite direction, extending strong facility-
level positions deeper into the data hall. Lite-On remains more concentrated around 
conversion and rack power, leaving meaningful upside if it successfully expands into 
centralized power racks and SST, but also greater risk if value migrates upstream faster 
than its product portfolio broadens.

What increasingly determines competitive advantage
As AI power systems move from tens of kilowatts per rack toward several hundred 
kilowatts and ultimately megawatt-class systems, we see five factors becoming 
increasingly important.
1. Platform qualification and execution remain critical. Suppliers need to be 
designed into NVIDIA, AMD and hyperscaler reference platforms before the major 
volume ramp and then demonstrate reliable manufacturing execution across 
rapidly changing generations.
2. Second, power-density engineering becomes a larger barrier to entry. 
Moving from 5.5kW PSU modules toward 12-18kW-class modules, hundreds-of-
kW power shelves and eventually multi-MW power systems requires higher 
efficiency, stronger transient performance, thermal management, redundancy and 
coordinated system controls.
3. Third, breadth across the power BOM becomes increasingly important. Our 
TAM work shows that value is progressively distributed across AC/DC conversion, 
storage, HVDC distribution, protection, downstream DC/DC conversion, controls 
and cooling rather than remaining concentrated in a single PSU line item.
4. Fourth, suppliers need the ability to follow value upstream. The transition 
from integrated 48/54V racks toward ±400V/800V power racks, centralized 
power centers and eventually medium-voltage rectification or SST shifts a larger 
portion of the opportunity toward engineered systems outside the IT rack.
5. Finally, global scale, qualification history and field support become more 
important as power per deployment increases. Hyperscalers are unlikely to 
select suppliers based only on component price when individual power systems 
support hundreds of thousands or millions of dollars of compute. Reliability, 
geographic manufacturing diversity, commissioning capability, controls and long-
term service therefore become increasingly relevant competitive differentiators.
These dynamics generally favor incumbents with both deep power-electronics expertise 
and broad system portfolios, while leaving room for focused rack-power suppliers to 
outperform if they successfully expand content faster than the architecture migrates 
upstream.
These competitive positions are increasingly visible in vendors’ relative scale, growth and 
financial capacity. To compare companies with different reporting structures, we use the 
closest disclosed power- and infrastructure-related revenue category for each supplier. 
The comparison is therefore directional rather than strictly like-for-like, but it illustrates 
the resources available to fund product development, platform qualification, capacity 
and field support.

Grey-space incumbents increasingly move toward the rack
Vertiv, Schneider and Eaton approach the opportunity from the opposite side of the 
value chain. Their established positions are in UPS, switchgear, facility distribution, 
protection and large-scale power infrastructure rather than traditional server PSUs. The 
move toward 800V DC power centers and eventually multi-MW rectifier or SST blocks is 
strategically favorable because

it shifts more of the AI power BOM into systems where 

engineering, protection, commissioning, software, controls and field service are as 
important as component cost.
 Vertiv appears especially well positioned where high-density power and cooling 
converge. Its portfolio across UPS, distribution, rack PDUs, power shelves, CDUs 
and liquid cooling provides a natural path toward integrated 800V sidecars and 
centralized megawatt-scale power systems. As AI deployments become 
increasingly constrained by both electrical and thermal density, this combined 
power-and-cooling position could become more valuable.
 Schneider Electric benefits from deep capability in switchgear, power distribution 
and controls through its EcoStruxure platform. Centralized HVDC power centers 
fit naturally with its broader data-center systems position, particularly where 
customers prefer a single vendor to integrate facility electrical infrastructure, 
control systems and increasingly rack-adjacent power conversion.
 Eaton brings strong North American medium- and low-voltage distribution, 
protection and power-quality expertise. Its opportunity should rise as conversion 
moves toward larger HVDC systems and potentially medium-voltage rectification 
or SST. Relative to Delta or Lite-On, however, Eaton has less historical content 
immediately adjacent to the accelerator, making the transition more dependent on 
its ability to extend into the white space.
Flex and other integration-led competitors
 Flex competes differently from the pure-play power suppliers. It offers large-scale 
EMS/ODM integration and the ability to combine power, cooling, racks and 
manufacturing into complete systems. The 2026 acquisition of Electrical Power 
Products expands its ability to provide utility-level infrastructure. Flex is among the 
four primary vendors for Vera Rubin power content alongside Delta, Lite-On and 
Megmeet.
 Advanced Energy and AcBel remain more specialized participants. Advanced 
Energy has highest exposure in high-performance custom conversion where 
efficiency, density and control requirements can support premium solutions rather 
than high-volume commodity rack power. AcBel has power-conversion expertise 
and could participate selectively in AI rack power, but its narrower platform 
exposure and smaller system portfolio make broad share gains less certain.
China suppliers are progressing, but barriers to hyperscale share gains 
remain
Chinese power suppliers continue to improve in PSU, rectification and high-voltage 
conversion and remain an important longer-term source of pricing competition. 
However, high-density AI systems are becoming less commodity-like as rack power 
increases. Customers place substantial value on transient performance, fault tolerance, 
qualification history, global supply assurance, safety compliance and field reliability.
We expect Chinese suppliers including Megmeet to gain first through components, and 
programs with short lead time given their quick responsiveness with first order at a 
major AI native given short lead time. Over time, successful qualification in 800V power 
racks and high-power PSU platforms would increase competitive pressure, particularly 
on mature conversion products. However, the broader system opportunity in protection, 
controls, storage and HVDC distribution should make competitive share shifts slower 
than simple PSU price comparisons imply.

Delta Electronics: broadest exposure across the architecture transition
We see Delta as one of the best-positioned suppliers across the transition because its 
opportunity extends well beyond conventional server PSUs. Delta participates in AC/DC 
power conversion, rack power shelves, BBU/CBU, DC/DC conversion, HVDC power 
racks, distribution, controls and liquid cooling, while its industrial power capabilities 
create a path toward medium-voltage conversion, SST and microgrid architectures.
This breadth is particularly important in the context of our TAM analysis. As AI systems 
transition from integrated 48/54V architectures toward dedicated power racks and 
ultimately more centralized facility-level conversion, value does not simply disappear 
from the power chain. Instead, content migrates toward higher-voltage rectification, 
storage, HVDC distribution, protection, control and higher-ratio downstream 
conversion. Delta’s portfolio gives it the ability to participate across these transitions 
rather than depending on a single architecture.
We therefore view Delta as relatively architecture agnostic. It can monetize continued 
adoption of integrated 48/54V power shelves, participate in ±400V/800V rack-side 
power systems, move upstream into larger power centers and potentially capture 
incremental content from SST or other medium-voltage conversion architectures. Its 
liquid-cooling portfolio also gives it additional exposure as power and thermal 
management become increasingly interdependent at higher rack densities.

The key risks are different from those of a narrower PSU supplier. As the unit of sale 
becomes larger and moves further into the grey space, Delta faces more direct 
competition from Vertiv, Schneider, Eaton and other facility-power incumbents. 
Successful execution therefore increasingly depends not only on component 
performance but also on system-level integration, controls, service and qualification for 
multi-MW deployments.
Maintain Buy on Delta with a NT$2,750 Target 
We maintain our Buy rating and NT$2,750 target based on 35x average 2027-28 P/E, 
high-end of its range but reflecting higher growth and better margins versus its history. 
We keep earnings intact for 2026-27 at NT$42.30/NT$67.50 based on the company 
sales growing +41%/40% YoY with positive operating leverage to lift OpM from 
15.1%  2025 to 18.5%/21.1% in 2026-27.   We view our growth expectations 
appropriate and broadly in-line with its addressable power TAM the next few years 
keeping its market share around 40%.  The company should leverage its strong product 
line, R&D and field support to participate in the key power architecture transitions in the 
coming years moving the power stack out of the rack and also developing emerging 
nascent technologies including SST for facility level power transformation and 
rectification and fuel cells licensing Ceres for medium-term opportunity to supplement 
the power grid constraint with alternative energy.

Lite-On: a stronger contender in AI power
Lite-On has spent several years exiting lower-return businesses, improving its margin 
structure and redirecting investment toward Cloud & AIoT, where AI server power is now 
becoming a meaningful growth and earnings driver. AI server PSU shipments began 
ramping in late 2024/2025, customer qualifications have broadened, and the company 
is moving beyond individual power modules into larger power shelves, BBU/energy-
management systems and eventually dedicated high-voltage power racks. Importantly, 
our checks suggest the power-rack opportunity is already becoming tangible on custom 

ASICs: we expect Lite-On to begin ramping a dedicated 48V power rack for its top 
ASIC client from late 2026, before stepping up to an ~800V/MW-class architecture with 
the following generation from late 2027. Lite-On remains well behind Delta in absolute 
AI power scale and breadth, but our forecasts do not require it to close that gap. The 
base case assumes only modest GPU-server share and stronger positions in selected 
custom-ASIC programs, leaving additional CSP wins as upside rather than a prerequisite.
Lite-On has improved execution, securing NVIDIA approved-vendor qualification and 
supplying three of the top five CSPs, with a leading position in power supplies for 
Trainium ASIC servers. Our checks point to a first dedicated 48V ASIC power rack ramp 
from late 2026, followed by a substantially higher-content 800V/MW-class architecture 
with the next generation from late 2027. We also expect penetration into the remaining 
two hyperscalers within 12–18 months. Cloud & AIoT revenue growth accelerated from 
-2% in 2024 to +48% in 2025 and +60% in 2026 YTD as design wins ramped. Sharper 
business focus and R&D investment are strengthening its platforms for upcoming 
transitions, including dedicated power racks. Supported by its balance sheet and near-
term capacity expansion, we believe Lite-On can sustain a top-three position in data-
centre white-space power and capture strong AI market growth.
Initiate Lite-On with a Buy and NT$400 Target 
We expect Lite-On to capture more of the expanding AI power electronics opportunity 
as execution improves, its customer base broadens and margins rise. Cloud power (48% 
of our 2026 sales forecast) should benefit from higher content per watt alongside 
growth in GW of AI hardware deployed. We initiate with a Buy and NT$400 target, 
implying 25x 2027E EPS versus peers at 29x. Our NT$400 price target applies 20x to our 
2028E EPS of NT$20, equivalent to 25x our 2027E EPS of NT$16 versus peers at 29x. 
Lite-On has historically traded at 8–14x P/E, but we believe its transition into a key AI 
power supplier warrants a higher multiple.

Sector implications
AI Data Center Power Semis: Francois-Xavier Bouvignies 
Key message: AI data-centre power semiconductors are one of the strongest growth 
opportunities in analog, with the market rising from roughly $4bn in 2026E to around 
$15bn by 2029-30E. However, the required pace of data-centre capacity additions is 
well above broader infrastructure forecasts, increasing the risk of a digestion period. We 
prefer prospective share gainers over incumbent leaders already discounting strong 
execution.
Revamped BoM estimates and higher units estimates drives TAM higher
Alongside this report, we update (link) our forecast for the AI power semis TAM to US
$13bn by 2028E vs. US$11bn previously, rising to US$15bn in 2030, driven by higher 
custom ASICs power semis revenue and higher rack estimates across GPU and custom 
ASIC racks from UBS Taiwan Hardware team. We have expanded our bill of materials 
estimates to 30+ xPU generations, beyond the six GPU configurations we previously 
modelled. We have also adjusted component count to align rack configurations with 
UBS' Taiwan Hardware team and refined ASP estimates based on deep dives on the 
shifting product architecture of each power stage.
Our new estimates drive a content per GW range of $100-200m/GW and an average 
rising from $95m/GW in 2024 to $126m/GW in 2026E and $130-140m/GW beyond. 
Implied GW additions suggest potential for a digestion period
Our estimates imply c60GW of capacity added in 2027, increasing steadily to c110GW 
in 2030, vs market expectations of c30-50GW annually. Cumulatively our estimates 
imply 370GW of capacity additions from 2026-2030E vs. <250GW in a 30-50W 
scenario. This also compares to <100GW of power grid additions in the US over the 
same period, though the delta could be bridged with behind-the-meter generation. 
Altogether we see an increasing likelihood of some digestion in power semis. While 
power semiconductor lead times are rising, we view electrical infrastructure as a larger 
bottleneck to AI buildout. Lead times for backup power systems and switchgear extend 
to ~18 months and beyond 3 years for utility scale transformers and on-site gas turbines.

How to play the theme: Prefer TI, ADI, and STM over Infineon 
Given the potential for some level of digestion, we would take a selective approach to 
playing the theme. We are cautious on market share leaders such as Infineon (Neutral), 
given high investor expectations and increasing competition. We prefer potential market 
share winners with spare capacity, bringing new products to markets where they are not 
currently present such as TI (Buy) with PSUs and IBCs and Analog Devices (Buy) with 
VRMs. We also prefer stories where power is upside rather than core to the thesis, such 
as STMicro (Buy) with its photonics exposure.

MLCC:  Shingo Hirata and Jimmy Yoon
Rising AI power a significant opportunity for MLCCs
We believe rising AI-related power requirements represent a significant growth 
opportunity for MLCC suppliers and will further accelerate the industry's migration 
toward higher-end products. To date, MLCC content growth has been driven primarily 
by compute boards, where content per system increased by approximately 5-10x with 
the transition from conventional servers to AI servers. We continue to see additional 
content expansion as the industry migrates to next-generation GPU and ASIC server 
racks.
Power content to expand with 800V and SST architectural migration
While the contribution from AI power applications remains relatively small compared 
with compute boards, we believe this represents a meaningful incremental growth 
opportunity for MLCCs as server power consumption continues to increase. 
Furthermore, architectural changes such as the adoption of 800V HVDC and solid-state 
transformers (SSTs) should create not only additional MLCC content opportunities but 
also a more favorable product mix, given the increasing need for higher-voltage MLCCs.
Capacity freed up by the EV slowdown can be deployed to AI power 
Our recent discussions with TDK (JP6762) suggest that the company has started to see AI 
power MLCC revenue growing at more than 100% YoY, albeit from a relatively small 
base compared with its overall MLCC business. Management indicated that the 
slowdown in the EV market has freed up capacity, enabling the company to 
accommodate rapidly growing demand from AI power applications. Given the stringent 
reliability requirements of AI power systems, MLCC suppliers with a strong track record 
in xEV powertrain applications should be particularly well positioned to benefit. TDK 
estimates that it currently holds a 30-40% share of the AI power MLCC market. We 
believe robust demand for AI power MLCCs could increasingly drive capacity 
reallocation away from automotive powertrain applications. This could contribute to 
tighter supply-demand conditions across the broader MLCC market and potentially 
support future pricing improvements.
Energy Storage (BBU / CBU): Tim Bush and Kenji Yasui
What a hyperscaler uses batteries for
A hyperscaler cannot let chips go dark. There are two backups: First, a short backup in or 
next to the rack that covers a power dip from a fraction of a second to a few minutes so 
the rack stays up while building power supply recovers. The battery back up unit (BBU) 
and the faster capacitor back up unit (CBU) play this role. Second, the building (data-
centre hall) covers a longer outage until generators start, and can run for hours. This is 

an uninterruptive power supply (UPS), or hall battery system. 
Why the rack changes this
Older Hopper racks pulled high current at low voltage. The 800-volt Rubin design cuts 
current and  lets voltage step down closer to the chips. Backup systems can now sit in a 
power cabinet (sidecar)  beside the IT rack instead of inside every Hopper style server tray. 
Some sites will still put a BBU  in the sidecar. Others will lean on the building UPS and 
keep only small, fast buffers at the rack. That is the operators' choice. Our working case 
for Rubin-class systems is about half still take a rack BBU. 
BBU market $2.5bn in 2026, to $13bn by 2030
The BBU market is the battery next to / in the rack, not the building UPS.  BBU sales 
should rise from $0.7bn in 2025 to $2.5bn in 2026 to $12.8bn by 2030. Nvidia is about  
$1.2bn of the 2026 total. Assuming a 5min duration and a BBU system cost of $0.2/W, 
we estimate that battery cells represent 10-15% of the BBU system cost. If we include 
the capacitor shelf the combined market (BBU + CBU) is $3.1bn in 2026 reaching 
$15.9bn in 2030. Growth in 2026-27 is more racks and more power per rack. Some 
investors treat Rubin as the end of BBU.  In our view, Rubin gradually moves the battery 
out of the tray, not off the floor. The 800-volt sidecar still has an optional BBU and model 
a 40-50% attach rate on Rubin class systems. Dollars of BBU per rack rise versus Hopper 
because the rack draws much more power. What can fall is cylindrical cells in the tray, 
not backup as a product. If a site leans on hall UPS, attach in sidecar drops. Total 
batteries on the floor can still rise. 
Positioning in battery - Panasonic leveraged to near rack side cars vs Samsung 
SDI driving toward the pooled storage opportunity
Panasonic is the compact rack product: cylindrical cells and full backup modules for the 
sidecar. Customers should keep buying that short duration  backup.  If reserve minutes 
move into the hall, cylindrical form factor in the tray could decline. Samsung SDI sell 
both rack cells and larger building batteries (UPS). In our view SDI could begin LFP for 
UPS at one of its two US expansion sites. They could be margin accretive with  onshore 
battery production: US cell production can receive production tax credit; overseas 
cylindrical lines do not.

Valuation Method and Risk Statement
Investing in the technology sector involves a high degree of risk. Rapid technological changes, 
increasing competition and exposure to macroeconomic cycles are among the many risks 
faced by investors in tech stocks. Moreover, it is extremely difficult to project the financial 
results of tech companies since their operating models are highly volatile and unpredictable. 
Finally, valuing tech stocks can prove challenging as neither traditional nor non-traditional 
valuation measures provide much insight into how these stocks trade. 
Delta: We base our price target on PE multiple valuation. 
Delta's businesses include SPS and components for a variety of end-applications, video 
displays and data networking subsystem and system products. Any changes in these end-
markets could affect our forecasts for Delta. Investment risk could increase/decrease on any 
deviation from our expectations for end-market demand and competition. 
Downside risks for Delta include: severe supply chain constraints; weaker-than-expected PC/ 
server demand; a slower-than-expected IA recovery; and a slower ramp of 5G in 2022.
Megmeet: We value Megmeet based on SOTP methodology. 
Downside risks for the company include: 1) structural price and supply risks of key raw 
materials, including semiconductors, magnetic components, passive components, structural 
parts, and PCBs. As direct materials account for >80% of COGS, raw material price 
fluctuations and S/D dynamics are the main factors affecting production costs; 2) 
undershooting demand -- disappointing AI development could be a drag on earnings; 3) 
changes in technical routes -- persisting uncertainties in AI power supply technology routes 
could weigh on earnings; 4) geopolitical tensions and changes in the international trade 
environment -- geopolitics and FX volatility could also affect earnings given rising overseas 
revenue exposure. 
Upside risks for the company includes: 1) accelerated market share gain in Nvidia ecosystem 
for AI server power supplies; 2) faster R&D and adoption of 800V DC power products; 3) 
better-than-expected mass production execution and capacity ramp-up.
Lite-On: We value Lite-On Technology using PE methodology. Key risks to our investment 
thesis:
The principal risk is a slower AI infrastructure deployment cycle. Our industry work shows 
deployed IT GW is the single-largest determinant of the power TAM, so a meaningful 
reduction in hyperscaler accelerator deployment would affect all power suppliers.
Customer concentration is a second risk, particularly Lite-On’s large custom-ASIC exposure 
and reliance on a relatively small number of hyperscalers. Program delays or share changes 
can materially affect annual revenue.
Execution on capacity expansion also matters. Lite-On is investing substantially ahead of 
forecast demand; if utilization ramps more slowly, depreciation and fixed operating costs 
could limit expected margin improvement.
Competitive pricing remains a risk as more suppliers qualify for high-power products. We 
believe the move toward larger, more engineered modules and systems should moderate 
pure commodity pricing pressure, but it will not eliminate it.
Architecture is another source of uncertainty. A slower transition to external power racks is 
not particularly damaging to our near-term thesis because 48/54V systems still require 
substantial power content. Longer term, however, the precise mix between rack-level BBUs, 
pooled UPS/BESS, ±400V, single-bus 800V and facility-level conversion will determine where 
value accrues within the supply chain.
Rising competition and slower spec upgrades would impact earnings. Faster progress from 
Chinese power suppliers, FX movements and weaker legacy IT/consumer demand could 
create additional earnings variability.

SST adoption also represents an expansion and a redistribution of the power-content
opportunity. In our RF200 scenario, approximately US$706k of upstream SST content is
partly offset by lower conventional front-end conversion content, producing a net
system-content increase of approximately US$381k. The supplier opportunity depends
on capturing good market share on that key transition to more than offset the displaced
content near the IT rack.
Turning the BOM into content per watt gives us a common
denominator
For every platform we calculate power-system content per rack and divide it by the IT
watts supported by that system. This produces a platform-specific content-per-watt
metric that allows a 100kW integrated rack, an 800kW power-rack architecture and a
future megawatt-class system to be compared on the same basis. Blended content/W
reflects both architecture-specific changes in the required hardware and shifts in
deployment mix across platforms; it should not be interpreted as like-for-like pricing for
existing power products.
At the aggregate industry level, blended content increases from approximately US$0.57/
W in 2025 to US$0.67/W in 2026, US$0.75/W in 2027, US$0.81/W in 2028, US$0.86/W
in 2029 and US$0.87/W in 2030, maintaining a healthy 9% CAGR from 2025-30.
Architecture-driven content expansion came first from moves to rack scale systems such
as Blackwell in 2025-26 and upcoming AMD Helios in 2027 followed by the transition to
higher-density, externally powered 400/800V systems through 2028-29.   Because 1GW
of IT load at US$1/W of content equals US$1bn of TAM, the final calculation is
transparent:  AI power TAM = annual AI IT GW deployed × blended power-system
content per IT watt.
Strong 2027 growth does not depend on widespread 800V power-rack
adoption
We see 2026–27 as the principal TAM inflection, as rising accelerator units coincide with
higher rack density and an architecture-driven increase in content per watt. TAM nearly
triples in 2026 to US$17.7bn and more than doubles again to US$38.2bn in 2027.
The 2027 opportunity does not require widespread adoption of native 800V
architectures. In our model, annual AI IT capacity rises approximately  92%, while
blended power content per watt increases approximately 12%, together driving
115% TAM growth. The principal drivers are the scale of accelerator deployments and
rising system power supplemented by richer power-system content.  We expect a strong
year driven by the aggressive sourcing plans for accelerator growth including strong
Google TPU and Amazon Trainium forecasts, still strong power content growth with
Rubin TDP 60% above Blackwell and AMD moving to a rack scale system with high
power electronics content.
The slower initial transition by NVIDIA would shift more of that architecture-driven
content opportunity into 2028-29 which could at that time offset some of the
moderation of AI capex. We view Rubin Ultra having only mild upgrade with 30%
penetration in our base case with modest TDP expansion from 225kW to 250kW but
likely ramping sharply with the Feynman generation in late 2028 as that has much
higher chance to move to 4 GPUs per package and 288+ GPUs per rack.

For custom ASICs, we expect Google and Meta to have about 30% of their 2027 ramps
of TPUv8 and MTIA v4 with 400V power racks while Amazon would shift similar mix to a
48V power rack.  With Google designing to EMIB-T and 4 dies on its v9 TPU with
Mediatek and Amazon a 4 die design for Trainium 4 with Alchip, we model those
transitioning to power racks in 2028.
While growth moderates, the power track transition keeps the TAM expanding. TAM
rises to US$55.1bn in 2028, US$75.8bn in 2029 and US$91.1bn in 2030, representing
annual dollar additions of approximately US$16.9bn, US$20.7bn and US$15.3bn,
respectively. We view this as a transition from an early units + density + architecture
growth phase toward a later primarily watts growth phase although still a swing factor
around architecture upgrades.
Figure 47: AI power TAM growth moderates after 2027, but annual dollar
increases remain substantial
Source: UBS
Upside to our out-year estimates would come from higher supported IT power, a richer
architecture mix, greater storage attachment or higher SST penetration than assumed.
The extent to which these raise total TAM depends on the additional hardware required
rather than density alone.
We would note our TAM covers the power hardware identified in our rack and allocated
power-rack BOMs including upstream SST content where modeled for Rosa-Feynman. It
is not an estimate of total data-center electrical capital expenditure which would include
more of the grey zone equipment.
NVIDIA 800V ramp may start slowly; ASIC power upgrades broaden the
opportunity
NVIDIA provides perhaps the cleanest illustration of the model mechanics. Within our
NVL72+ category, physical rack shipments are approximately 27,000 in both 2025 and
2030—essentially no endpoint unit growth. Yet the average system advances from
approximately 125kW to 1.2MW if NVIDIA gets to 576 GPUs within a rack by 2030,
increasing annual deployed IT capacity from 3.4GW to 32.4GW. At the same time, our
blended content assumption for NVL72 racks rises from approximately US$0.59/W to US
$1.04/W as the architecture adds richer conversion, energy storage, high-voltage
distribution and rack infrastructure.  The resulting annual power TAM grows from
approximately US$2.0bn in 2025 to US$33.6bn in 2030, despite essentially flat
endpoint rack units.  We apply the same framework to HGX, CPU and LPU racks for a
total NVIDIA power TAM scaling from US$3.7bn in 2025 to US$41.8bn in 2030.

Power TAM growth does not depend on a strong initial
NVIDIA migration to 800V
The market has focused on the slower migration to 800V and dedicated power racks for
Rubin, as approximately 440kW of 54V power shelves within the IT rack can support a
227kW Oberon NVL72 system. Our checks suggest initial power-rack penetration has
moved lower as the existing architecture can extend through this generation and
additional time is required to qualify the new high-voltage architecture. The uncertainty
extends to Rubin Ultra, where a less aggressive upgrade than the original Kyber concept
could similarly defer the need for external power conversion. A mix of higher GPU power
and bandwidth but lower memory stack at 8 high nets to only a mild power upgrade to
250kW.
Importantly, our sensitivity analysis suggests this is a much smaller risk to the overall
power TAM than to the 800V narrative. Around our 2027 base case, each 10ppt change
in NVIDIA power-rack penetration changes total AI power TAM by only approximately
1%. The larger drivers are the roughly 92% increase in annual AI IT GW deployed and
higher power content across the broader market, including Rubin’s higher TDP , AMD’s
move toward rack-scale systems and initial adoption of power racks across custom ASIC
platforms. Strong 2027 TAM therefore does not require NVIDIA to lead the 800V
transition.

NVIDIA is also not the only path to externalized power. We expect Google and Meta to
begin adopting ±400V architectures on a portion of their 2027 deployments, while
Amazon can continue scaling a lower-voltage architecture with a 48V power rack before
transitioning to 800V with Trainium 4 in 2028. The timing and topology differ, but the
common direction is toward higher rack power, greater centralization of conversion and
richer distribution/protection content.
For 2028, we do see a more mild ramp on Rubin Ultra followed by a strong adoption of
power racks or initial SST shipments from late 2028 with the Feynman generation likely
moving to 4+ dies and 288+ GPUs per rack and supporting 800V power side car. We
model a 30% penetration and around our base case, each 15ppt change in Rubin Ultra
power-rack penetration changes total power TAM by approximately 1.3–1.4%. We
model only a moderate initial NVIDIA power-rack ramp, leaving meaningful upside if
adoption occurs faster, while limiting downside from a slower transition.
By 2028, industry TAM is increasingly diversified beyond NVIDIA architecture decisions.
We expect stronger power-system upgrades across Google, Amazon and other ASIC

platforms to support industry TAM even as NVIDIA enters a comparatively modest Rubin
Ultra upgrade year. This diversification helps sustain our 44% total AI power TAM
growth to US$55.1bn in 2028 despite slower NVIDIA growth.

GPU and ASIC power remain nearly equally important
Our bottom-up model is also built up for AMD and each major ASIC customer rather
than applying NVIDIA economics across the industry. Chips per rack, system power, BBU/
CBU architecture, high-voltage topology, dedicated power-rack requirements and
component content all vary by customer.  We estimate GPU systems from NVIDIA and
AMD represent approximately 59% of AI power TAM in 2025, 58% in 2026 and 56% in
2027, before falling to approximately 51% in 2028 and ending at 54% in 2030. ASIC
systems therefore represent roughly 40–50% of industry power TAM throughout most
of the forecast.
In dollar terms, GPU power TAM rises from US$3.9bn in 2025 to US$49.2bn in 2030,
while ASIC power TAM increases from US$2.7bn to US$42.0bn. The architectures differ
—AWS, Google, Meta, Microsoft and OpenAI will not necessarily converge on NVIDIA’s
exact rack implementation—but the fundamental power problem is common: more
accelerator watts require greater conversion, protection, distribution, storage/
smoothing and downstream voltage conversion while the move up in rack compute
density through more dies per package and more chips per rack is driving the
OCP standards move toward power racks and native 800VDC architectures like NVIDIA.
This breadth is important for the investment case. The power TAM is ultimately tied to
industry AI watts deployed, rather than requiring any single GPU vendor, ASIC program
or rack standard to dominate the market. We would be explicit that the largest
uncertainties are not all in the same direction. Accelerator shipment timing can move
rack deployment between years; accelerators per rack can reduce rack counts even
while increasing watts per rack; package and system TDP can move the GW
denominator materially; and BBU/CBU attachment, power-rack sharing ratios, ±400V
versus single-bus 800V topology and eventual SST penetration can all change content
per watt.

The 169% and 115% growth rates we currently estimate for 2026 and 2027 could shift
with product ramps without changing the central conclusion: the AI power market is
moving from tens of kilowatts per rack toward hundreds of kilowatts and ultimately
megawatt-class systems, while the architecture simultaneously adds new conversion,
protection, storage and distribution content.
The critical point is that our US$91bn estimate is not predicated on extrapolating today’s
rack BOM. It reflects a bottom-up view of how many accelerator systems are deployed,
how much power those systems consume, where the power electronics sit and what
hardware is required to deliver each IT watt through successive rack architectures.

AI Power TAM Sensitivities: IT GW is the primary TAM
driver; architecture determines the upside around it
The two principal sensitivities to our AI Power TAM are annual IT capacity deployed and
power-system content per supported IT watt. At a constant content per watt, a 10%
change in our 104.5GW 2030 deployment assumption changes TAM by approximately
US$9.1bn. Conversely, at our modelled 104.5GW of annual IT deployments, a US$0.05/
W change in blended power-system content changes 2030 TAM by approximately US
$5.2bn.
The sensitivities are not completely independent. Higher rack power can increase IT GW
while simultaneously changing the required power architecture and therefore content
per watt; conversely, slower deployment of high-density systems can reduce both the
GW denominator and penetration of more content-rich power racks. We therefore view
the sensitivity tables as illustrating the magnitude of individual drivers.
Near-term TAM is most sensitive to IT GW deployed
Our 2027 base case assumes 50.8GW of annual IT capacity and US$0.75 of power-
system content per IT watt, producing approximately US$38.2bn of TAM. Around this
base case, each incremental 1GW of IT deployments adds roughly US$0.75bn of annual
TAM, or approximately 2% of the TAM level. A US$0.01/W change in blended content
adds approximately US$0.5bn, or around 1.3%.
The impact on the year-on-year growth rate is larger because the 2026 TAM base
remains relatively small. An additional 1GW in 2027 adds approximately 4.2 percentage
points to TAM growth, while an additional US$0.01/W of content adds approximately
2.9 percentage points. This reinforces our view that the magnitude and timing of AI
hardware deployments remain the most important variables for the 2026–27 inflection;
widespread native 800V adoption is not required for a strong 2027 outcome.

Component price erosion is a risk, but rising system power and
architectural upgrades mitigate the impact
Competitive pricing is another risk as conventional PSU volumes scale, more suppliers
qualify and mature specifications such as Blackwell's mainstream 5.5kW PSUs become
more standardized. However, our bottom-up BOM suggests that single-component
price erosion has a more modest effect on total system content than changes in IT GW or
architecture, because power content is increasingly distributed across conversion,
storage, protection, distribution, controls and downstream DC/DC and also the PSUs are
upgrading to higher complexity specs moving to 18.3kW and beyond.
Our VR200 integrated-power case contains approximately US$170k of rack power
content using a PSU-module assumption of roughly US$0.13/W and BBU content of
roughly US$0.20/W. Reducing PSU pricing by US$0.02/W lowers modelled rack power
content by approximately 5%, while a US$0.05/W reduction in BBU pricing reduces
total rack content by approximately 4%.
For the investment case, conventional PSU pricing on mature generations can face
competitive pressure without invalidating the broader power TAM, particularly as
additional content pools emerge in high-voltage distribution, protection, energy storage
and near-silicon conversion. For individual suppliers unable to gain early qualification on
newer generations of hardware, however, price erosion can still have a larger earnings
impact depending on product mix and market share.

Storage attachment is a larger architectural swing factor than storage
pricing alone
BBU and CBU content is less standardized than front-end conversion because
attachment depends on the resilience architecture selected by the data-center operator.
A deployment retaining centralized UPS infrastructure may need relatively little rack-
level battery capacity, while hyperscale systems requiring local ride-through or source-
transfer support may attach materially more storage.
For VR200, our base case assumes roughly 50% BBU attachment at US$0.20/W. At that
assumption, attach-weighted BBU content is approximately US$25.6k per system,
contributing materially to the roughly US$170k total power BOM. Holding BBU pricing
constant, moving attachment from 50% to 30% lowers modeled rack content by
approximately 6%, while increasing attachment to 70% raises content by a similar
amount. Moving across the much wider 10–100% attachment range produces a
materially larger swing.
We therefore view BBU penetration as an architectural assumption rather than simply
another ASP assumption. Greater upstream pooling of storage represents downside to
rack-level BBU attachment, while increasing requirements for local ride-through, fast
source transfer and workload stability provide upside. Importantly, lower rack-level BBU
content does not necessarily imply proportionately lower total data-center storage
content if capacity is instead centralized into DC UPS or BESS.

SST adoption is the largest out-year architecture sensitivity
The largest architecture-specific swing in our 2030 NVIDIA model is SST penetration.
Our base case assumes approximately 45% SST penetration, resulting in NVIDIA power
TAM of approximately US$41.8bn in 2030. Holding the underlying hardware forecast
constant, eliminating SST adoption reduces modelled NVIDIA TAM to approximately US
$37.2bn, while increasing penetration to 90% raises TAM to approximately US$46.4bn
under our base SST-content assumption.
The 45% SST assumption contributes roughly US$4.6bn of incremental NVIDIA power
TAM versus a no-SST scenario. Each additional 15ppt of SST penetration around our
base case moves annual TAM by roughly US$1.5bn, although the precise impact varies
with the assumed power content of an SST-equipped architecture.

SST penetration also has a disproportionate effect on the out-year growth profile. At our
base content assumption, 2030 NVIDIA TAM growth is approximately 24% with 45%
SST penetration, versus roughly 10% without SST adoption and approximately 38% at
90% penetration.
This highlights why we treat SST separately from our nearer-term 800V thesis: 2026–27
growth is driven primarily by rapidly rising IT GW and rack power, 2028-29 by power
rack upgrades and the 2029–30 and beyond growth profile is increasingly sensitive to
which architecture ultimately wins and how much upstream transformation content
migrates into the power-electronics opportunity.
SST should also be viewed as a net-content rather than gross-content opportunity. As
discussed earlier, some upstream SST value displaces conventional front-end rectification
and transformation. The relevant investment question is therefore not only whether SST
is adopted, but which suppliers capture the larger engineered system as value migrates
upstream and which are more impacted by displaced power conversion content closer to
the rack.

Near-term TAM is driven by GW; architecture matters increasingly in the
out-years
The sensitivity work reinforces three conclusions:
1. IT GW deployed remains the largest determinant of total TAM, particularly
through the 2026–27 ramp.
2. A broader power BOM limits the impact of competitive price erosion in any
individual component, particularly for vendors able to migrate toward newer,
higher-content architectures.
3. Architecture increasingly determines the out-years opportunity: storage
attachment, external power-rack penetration and particularly SST can materially
alter both content/watt and the distribution of value across suppliers.
Our US$91bn 2030 estimate does not require every platform to migrate to the most
content-rich architecture. Rather, the sensitivity work suggests the AI power thesis is
fundamentally a watts thesis first and an architecture thesis second: rising IT GW
expands the addressable market, while external power racks, storage and ultimately SST
determine how much incremental power-electronics content is captured around those
watts and which suppliers capture it.
Competitive landscape: who captures the
expanding AI power stack?
Convergence across the white-space and grey-space
The rapid increase in AI rack power is reshaping the competitive landscape across the
data-center power ecosystem. Historically, white-space suppliers focused on server
PSUs, rack-level power shelves and board-level conversion, while grey-space vendors
supplied UPS, switchgear, transformers and facility-level distribution. Higher-voltage DC
architectures increasingly blur this distinction. Bulk AC/DC conversion, energy storage,
protection and distribution progressively migrate upstream from the IT rack into
dedicated power racks, rows and ultimately facility-level systems, while high-ratio DC/

DC and point-of-load conversion move closer to the accelerator.
We therefore see competitive advantage shifting from leadership in an individual power
component toward breadth across the power stack, qualification with the major AI
platforms, system-level control capability and the ability to scale from rack-level products
into multi-MW power systems. Importantly, the opportunity does not accrue uniformly.
Some suppliers gain incremental content as new layers of power electronics are added,
while others risk having mature low-voltage conversion content displaced as conversion
becomes more centralized.

Historically the white-space and grey-space suppliers operated in relatively separate
parts of the data-center electrical chain. We expect that separation to narrow as higher-
voltage DC architectures mature. Grey-space incumbents are increasingly extending into
rack-adjacent HVDC systems, while leading white-space suppliers are moving upstream
into power racks, power centers and potentially medium-voltage conversion.
The key distinction therefore becomes less about where a supplier historically operated
and more about how many stages of the architecture transition it can monetize. Delta
has perhaps the broadest position spanning rack PSUs, DC/DC, energy storage, HVDC
power racks, thermal management and upstream power conversion. Vertiv, Schneider
and Eaton approach the market from the opposite direction, extending strong facility-
level positions deeper into the data hall. Lite-On remains more concentrated around
conversion and rack power, leaving meaningful upside if it successfully expands into
centralized power racks and SST, but also greater risk if value migrates upstream faster
than its product portfolio broadens.

What increasingly determines competitive advantage
As AI power systems move from tens of kilowatts per rack toward several hundred
kilowatts and ultimately megawatt-class systems, we see five factors becoming
increasingly important.
1. Platform qualification and execution remain critical. Suppliers need to be
designed into NVIDIA, AMD and hyperscaler reference platforms before the major
volume ramp and then demonstrate reliable manufacturing execution across
rapidly changing generations.
2. Second, power-density engineering becomes a larger barrier to entry.
Moving from 5.5kW PSU modules toward 12-18kW-class modules, hundreds-of-
kW power shelves and eventually multi-MW power systems requires higher
efficiency, stronger transient performance, thermal management, redundancy and
coordinated system controls.
3. Third, breadth across the power BOM becomes increasingly important. Our
TAM work shows that value is progressively distributed across AC/DC conversion,
storage, HVDC distribution, protection, downstream DC/DC conversion, controls
and cooling rather than remaining concentrated in a single PSU line item.
4. Fourth, suppliers need the ability to follow value upstream. The transition
from integrated 48/54V racks toward ±400V/800V power racks, centralized
power centers and eventually medium-voltage rectification or SST shifts a larger
portion of the opportunity toward engineered systems outside the IT rack.
5. Finally, global scale, qualification history and field support become more
important as power per deployment increases. Hyperscalers are unlikely to
select suppliers based only on component price when individual power systems
support hundreds of thousands or millions of dollars of compute. Reliability,
geographic manufacturing diversity, commissioning capability, controls and long-
term service therefore become increasingly relevant competitive differentiators.
These dynamics generally favor incumbents with both deep power-electronics expertise
and broad system portfolios, while leaving room for focused rack-power suppliers to
outperform if they successfully expand content faster than the architecture migrates
upstream.
These competitive positions are increasingly visible in vendors’ relative scale, growth and
financial capacity. To compare companies with different reporting structures, we use the
closest disclosed power- and infrastructure-related revenue category for each supplier.
The comparison is therefore directional rather than strictly like-for-like, but it illustrates
the resources available to fund product development, platform qualification, capacity
and field support.

Grey-space incumbents increasingly move toward the rack
Vertiv, Schneider and Eaton approach the opportunity from the opposite side of the
value chain. Their established positions are in UPS, switchgear, facility distribution,
protection and large-scale power infrastructure rather than traditional server PSUs. The
move toward 800V DC power centers and eventually multi-MW rectifier or SST blocks is
strategically favorable because
display.full_text_2:
it shifts more of the AI power BOM into systems where

engineering, protection, commissioning, software, controls and field service are as
important as component cost.
 Vertiv appears especially well positioned where high-density power and cooling
converge. Its portfolio across UPS, distribution, rack PDUs, power shelves, CDUs
and liquid cooling provides a natural path toward integrated 800V sidecars and
centralized megawatt-scale power systems. As AI deployments become
increasingly constrained by both electrical and thermal density, this combined
power-and-cooling position could become more valuable.
 Schneider Electric benefits from deep capability in switchgear, power distribution
and controls through its EcoStruxure platform. Centralized HVDC power centers
fit naturally with its broader data-center systems position, particularly where
customers prefer a single vendor to integrate facility electrical infrastructure,
control systems and increasingly rack-adjacent power conversion.
 Eaton brings strong North American medium- and low-voltage distribution,
protection and power-quality expertise. Its opportunity should rise as conversion
moves toward larger HVDC systems and potentially medium-voltage rectification
or SST. Relative to Delta or Lite-On, however, Eaton has less historical content
immediately adjacent to the accelerator, making the transition more dependent on
its ability to extend into the white space.
Flex and other integration-led competitors
 Flex competes differently from the pure-play power suppliers. It offers large-scale
EMS/ODM integration and the ability to combine power, cooling, racks and
manufacturing into complete systems. The 2026 acquisition of Electrical Power
Products expands its ability to provide utility-level infrastructure. Flex is among the
four primary vendors for Vera Rubin power content alongside Delta, Lite-On and
Megmeet.
 Advanced Energy and AcBel remain more specialized participants. Advanced
Energy has highest exposure in high-performance custom conversion where
efficiency, density and control requirements can support premium solutions rather
than high-volume commodity rack power. AcBel has power-conversion expertise
and could participate selectively in AI rack power, but its narrower platform
exposure and smaller system portfolio make broad share gains less certain.
China suppliers are progressing, but barriers to hyperscale share gains
remain
Chinese power suppliers continue to improve in PSU, rectification and high-voltage
conversion and remain an important longer-term source of pricing competition.
However, high-density AI systems are becoming less commodity-like as rack power
increases. Customers place substantial value on transient performance, fault tolerance,
qualification history, global supply assurance, safety compliance and field reliability.
We expect Chinese suppliers including Megmeet to gain first through components, and
programs with short lead time given their quick responsiveness with first order at a
major AI native given short lead time. Over time, successful qualification in 800V power
racks and high-power PSU platforms would increase competitive pressure, particularly
on mature conversion products. However, the broader system opportunity in protection,
controls, storage and HVDC distribution should make competitive share shifts slower
than simple PSU price comparisons imply.

The matrix highlights that no single supplier is strongest in every part of the stack.
Traditional white-space suppliers retain advantages closest to the compute rack, while
grey-space incumbents are better positioned as conversion migrates toward larger

bridge both sides of the architecture, or those with sufficient product momentum to
expand their addressable content faster than legacy products are displaced.
For our Taiwan coverage, this framework leaves Delta and Lite-On as the two most direct
beneficiaries, but with different risk/reward profiles. Delta offers broader architecture
exposure and greater protection against value migration, while Lite-On offers greater
operating leverage to continued rack-power share gains and successful expansion into

Delta Electronics: broadest exposure across the architecture transition
We see Delta as one of the best-positioned suppliers across the transition because its
opportunity extends well beyond conventional server PSUs. Delta participates in AC/DC
power conversion, rack power shelves, BBU/CBU, DC/DC conversion, HVDC power
racks, distribution, controls and liquid cooling, while its industrial power capabilities
create a path toward medium-voltage conversion, SST and microgrid architectures.
This breadth is particularly important in the context of our TAM analysis. As AI systems
transition from integrated 48/54V architectures toward dedicated power racks and
ultimately more centralized facility-level conversion, value does not simply disappear
from the power chain. Instead, content migrates toward higher-voltage rectification,
storage, HVDC distribution, protection, control and higher-ratio downstream
conversion. Delta’s portfolio gives it the ability to participate across these transitions
rather than depending on a single architecture.
We therefore view Delta as relatively architecture agnostic. It can monetize continued
adoption of integrated 48/54V power shelves, participate in ±400V/800V rack-side
power systems, move upstream into larger power centers and potentially capture
incremental content from SST or other medium-voltage conversion architectures. Its
liquid-cooling portfolio also gives it additional exposure as power and thermal
management become increasingly interdependent at higher rack densities.

The key risks are different from those of a narrower PSU supplier. As the unit of sale
becomes larger and moves further into the grey space, Delta faces more direct
competition from Vertiv, Schneider, Eaton and other facility-power incumbents.
Successful execution therefore increasingly depends not only on component
performance but also on system-level integration, controls, service and qualification for
multi-MW deployments.
Maintain Buy on Delta with a NT$2,750 Target
We maintain our Buy rating and NT$2,750 target based on 35x average 2027-28 P/E,
high-end of its range but reflecting higher growth and better margins versus its history.
We keep earnings intact for 2026-27 at NT$42.30/NT$67.50 based on the company
sales growing +41%/40% YoY with positive operating leverage to lift OpM from
15.1%  2025 to 18.5%/21.1% in 2026-27.   We view our growth expectations
appropriate and broadly in-line with its addressable power TAM the next few years
keeping its market share around 40%.  The company should leverage its strong product
line, R&D and field support to participate in the key power architecture transitions in the
coming years moving the power stack out of the rack and also developing emerging
nascent technologies including SST for facility level power transformation and
rectification and fuel cells licensing Ceres for medium-term opportunity to supplement
the power grid constraint with alternative energy.

Lite-On: a stronger contender in AI power
Lite-On has spent several years exiting lower-return businesses, improving its margin
structure and redirecting investment toward Cloud & AIoT, where AI server power is now
becoming a meaningful growth and earnings driver. AI server PSU shipments began
ramping in late 2024/2025, customer qualifications have broadened, and the company
is moving beyond individual power modules into larger power shelves, BBU/energy-
management systems and eventually dedicated high-voltage power racks. Importantly,
our checks suggest the power-rack opportunity is already becoming tangible on custom

ASICs: we expect Lite-On to begin ramping a dedicated 48V power rack for its top
ASIC client from late 2026, before stepping up to an ~800V/MW-class architecture with
the following generation from late 2027. Lite-On remains well behind Delta in absolute
AI power scale and breadth, but our forecasts do not require it to close that gap. The
base case assumes only modest GPU-server share and stronger positions in selected
custom-ASIC programs, leaving additional CSP wins as upside rather than a prerequisite.
Lite-On has improved execution, securing NVIDIA approved-vendor qualification and
supplying three of the top five CSPs, with a leading position in power supplies for
Trainium ASIC servers. Our checks point to a first dedicated 48V ASIC power rack ramp
from late 2026, followed by a substantially higher-content 800V/MW-class architecture
with the next generation from late 2027. We also expect penetration into the remaining
two hyperscalers within 12–18 months. Cloud & AIoT revenue growth accelerated from
-2% in 2024 to +48% in 2025 and +60% in 2026 YTD as design wins ramped. Sharper
business focus and R&D investment are strengthening its platforms for upcoming
transitions, including dedicated power racks. Supported by its balance sheet and near-
term capacity expansion, we believe Lite-On can sustain a top-three position in data-
centre white-space power and capture strong AI market growth.
Initiate Lite-On with a Buy and NT$400 Target
We expect Lite-On to capture more of the expanding AI power electronics opportunity
as execution improves, its customer base broadens and margins rise. Cloud power (48%
of our 2026 sales forecast) should benefit from higher content per watt alongside
growth in GW of AI hardware deployed. We initiate with a Buy and NT$400 target,
implying 25x 2027E EPS versus peers at 29x. Our NT$400 price target applies 20x to our
2028E EPS of NT$20, equivalent to 25x our 2027E EPS of NT$16 versus peers at 29x.
Lite-On has historically traded at 8–14x P/E, but we believe its transition into a key AI
power supplier warrants a higher multiple.

Sector implications
AI Data Center Power Semis: Francois-Xavier Bouvignies
Key message: AI data-centre power semiconductors are one of the strongest growth
opportunities in analog, with the market rising from roughly $4bn in 2026E to around
$15bn by 2029-30E. However, the required pace of data-centre capacity additions is
well above broader infrastructure forecasts, increasing the risk of a digestion period. We
prefer prospective share gainers over incumbent leaders already discounting strong
execution.
Revamped BoM estimates and higher units estimates drives TAM higher
Alongside this report, we update (link) our forecast for the AI power semis TAM to US
$13bn by 2028E vs. US$11bn previously, rising to US$15bn in 2030, driven by higher
custom ASICs power semis revenue and higher rack estimates across GPU and custom
ASIC racks from UBS Taiwan Hardware team. We have expanded our bill of materials
estimates to 30+ xPU generations, beyond the six GPU configurations we previously
modelled. We have also adjusted component count to align rack configurations with
UBS' Taiwan Hardware team and refined ASP estimates based on deep dives on the
shifting product architecture of each power stage.
Our new estimates drive a content per GW range of $100-200m/GW and an average
rising from $95m/GW in 2024 to $126m/GW in 2026E and $130-140m/GW beyond.
Implied GW additions suggest potential for a digestion period
Our estimates imply c60GW of capacity added in 2027, increasing steadily to c110GW
in 2030, vs market expectations of c30-50GW annually. Cumulatively our estimates
imply 370GW of capacity additions from 2026-2030E vs. <250GW in a 30-50W
scenario. This also compares to <100GW of power grid additions in the US over the
same period, though the delta could be bridged with behind-the-meter generation.
Altogether we see an increasing likelihood of some digestion in power semis. While
power semiconductor lead times are rising, we view electrical infrastructure as a larger
bottleneck to AI buildout. Lead times for backup power systems and switchgear extend
to ~18 months and beyond 3 years for utility scale transformers and on-site gas turbines.

How to play the theme: Prefer TI, ADI, and STM over Infineon
Given the potential for some level of digestion, we would take a selective approach to
playing the theme. We are cautious on market share leaders such as Infineon (Neutral),
given high investor expectations and increasing competition. We prefer potential market
share winners with spare capacity, bringing new products to markets where they are not
currently present such as TI (Buy) with PSUs and IBCs and Analog Devices (Buy) with
VRMs. We also prefer stories where power is upside rather than core to the thesis, such
as STMicro (Buy) with its photonics exposure.

MLCC:  Shingo Hirata and Jimmy Yoon
Rising AI power a significant opportunity for MLCCs
We believe rising AI-related power requirements represent a significant growth
opportunity for MLCC suppliers and will further accelerate the industry's migration
toward higher-end products. To date, MLCC content growth has been driven primarily
by compute boards, where content per system increased by approximately 5-10x with
the transition from conventional servers to AI servers. We continue to see additional
content expansion as the industry migrates to next-generation GPU and ASIC server
racks.
Power content to expand with 800V and SST architectural migration
While the contribution from AI power applications remains relatively small compared
with compute boards, we believe this represents a meaningful incremental growth
opportunity for MLCCs as server power consumption continues to increase.
Furthermore, architectural changes such as the adoption of 800V HVDC and solid-state
transformers (SSTs) should create not only additional MLCC content opportunities but
also a more favorable product mix, given the increasing need for higher-voltage MLCCs.
Capacity freed up by the EV slowdown can be deployed to AI power
Our recent discussions with TDK (JP6762) suggest that the company has started to see AI
power MLCC revenue growing at more than 100% YoY, albeit from a relatively small
base compared with its overall MLCC business. Management indicated that the
slowdown in the EV market has freed up capacity, enabling the company to
accommodate rapidly growing demand from AI power applications. Given the stringent
reliability requirements of AI power systems, MLCC suppliers with a strong track record
in xEV powertrain applications should be particularly well positioned to benefit. TDK
estimates that it currently holds a 30-40% share of the AI power MLCC market. We
believe robust demand for AI power MLCCs could increasingly drive capacity
reallocation away from automotive powertrain applications. This could contribute to
tighter supply-demand conditions across the broader MLCC market and potentially
support future pricing improvements.
Energy Storage (BBU / CBU): Tim Bush and Kenji Yasui
What a hyperscaler uses batteries for
A hyperscaler cannot let chips go dark. There are two backups: First, a short backup in or
next to the rack that covers a power dip from a fraction of a second to a few minutes so
the rack stays up while building power supply recovers. The battery back up unit (BBU)
and the faster capacitor back up unit (CBU) play this role. Second, the building (data-
centre hall) covers a longer outage until generators start, and can run for hours. This is

an uninterruptive power supply (UPS), or hall battery system.
Why the rack changes this
Older Hopper racks pulled high current at low voltage. The 800-volt Rubin design cuts
current and  lets voltage step down closer to the chips. Backup systems can now sit in a
power cabinet (sidecar)  beside the IT rack instead of inside every Hopper style server tray.
Some sites will still put a BBU  in the sidecar. Others will lean on the building UPS and
keep only small, fast buffers at the rack. That is the operators' choice. Our working case
for Rubin-class systems is about half still take a rack BBU.
BBU market $2.5bn in 2026, to $13bn by 2030
The BBU market is the battery next to / in the rack, not the building UPS.  BBU sales
should rise from $0.7bn in 2025 to $2.5bn in 2026 to $12.8bn by 2030. Nvidia is about
$1.2bn of the 2026 total. Assuming a 5min duration and a BBU system cost of $0.2/W,
we estimate that battery cells represent 10-15% of the BBU system cost. If we include
the capacitor shelf the combined market (BBU + CBU) is $3.1bn in 2026 reaching
$15.9bn in 2030. Growth in 2026-27 is more racks and more power per rack. Some
investors treat Rubin as the end of BBU.  In our view, Rubin gradually moves the battery
out of the tray, not off the floor. The 800-volt sidecar still has an optional BBU and model
a 40-50% attach rate on Rubin class systems. Dollars of BBU per rack rise versus Hopper
because the rack draws much more power. What can fall is cylindrical cells in the tray,
not backup as a product. If a site leans on hall UPS, attach in sidecar drops. Total
batteries on the floor can still rise.
Positioning in battery - Panasonic leveraged to near rack side cars vs Samsung
SDI driving toward the pooled storage opportunity
Panasonic is the compact rack product: cylindrical cells and full backup modules for the
sidecar. Customers should keep buying that short duration  backup.  If reserve minutes
move into the hall, cylindrical form factor in the tray could decline. Samsung SDI sell
both rack cells and larger building batteries (UPS). In our view SDI could begin LFP for
UPS at one of its two US expansion sites. They could be margin accretive with  onshore
battery production: US cell production can receive production tax credit; overseas
cylindrical lines do not.
